# Wrap-aware steering and clearance

Parent: "Bot should be aware of screen wrap around" (AH-0MVMISF0Q00314LG) — AC1.

## Goal (user story)

As a **player watching the attract demo**, I want the bot to cross a screen edge
to reach a target that is closer the other way, instead of treating the four
seam edges as walls it must not approach, so its movement looks like a human's
and it stops camping near walls it wrongly fears.

## Context

Both steering evaluators reject a bearing purely because it reaches an edge
inside `wallMargin`:

- legacy `evaluateVector` — `src/ai/botDecision.ts` ("reaches a wall within
  `wallMargin`", `wallMargin: 40` default);
- competent `evaluateDirection` — `src/ai/framework/competent/steering.ts`
  ("Walls: reject a bearing that reaches an edge inside the wall margin",
  `wallMargin: 30` default).

Both also derive the objective bearing from the raw straight line, so a
seam-crossing route to an objective is never even considered. The playfield
genuinely wraps: the player ship wraps at all four edges
(`src/utils/movementModel.ts`), bullets wrap (`src/scenes/core/bulletLifecycle.ts`),
and wrap-aware enemies now fly over the edges too (AH-0MV9G3DZ9003P7P8).

This slice consumes the primitives from the wrap-geometry child
(AH-0MVMISF0Q00314LG's wrap-geometry primitive child) — no seam maths is written
here.

## Scope

1. Remove the wall test from both evaluators: an edge is no longer a hazard, so
   `evaluateVector`/`evaluateDirection` never mark a bearing unsafe merely for
   reaching an edge. Keep clearance meaningful: the distance-to-edge term stays
   only as a *clearance* contribution if it is still useful, and if it is dropped
   the clearance cap semantics are preserved.
2. Steering objectives use the **shortest wrapped path**: the objective bearing
   fed to the fan is computed with the wrapped delta (raw vs. seam-crossing
   duplicate of the objective, whichever is shorter), with the near-tie
   hysteresis from the geometry child so the chosen duplicate does not flip
   every tick.
3. Edge-crossing motion is used deliberately when net-positive (Q2 in the
   parent Appendix) — it falls out of shortest-path selection; no scripted wrap
   manœuvre and no change to the human-like governor
   (`src/ai/botHumanLike.ts`).
4. Update the existing integration assertion in
   `src/ai/botSteering.integration.test.ts` that presumes the bot "never wraps
   the screen" (the brake-to-stop case) so it still asserts a controlled stop
   without asserting the bot cannot cross a seam; add seam scenarios instead.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. The four arena edges stop being walls in the steering safety/clearance test:
   neither the legacy `evaluateVector` (`src/ai/botDecision.ts`) nor the
   competent `evaluateDirection` (`src/ai/framework/competent/steering.ts`)
   rejects a direction solely because it reaches an edge within `wallMargin`; a
   unit test per evaluator drives a bearing straight at each of the four edges
   from mid-playfield and asserts `safe === true`.
2. Steering toward an objective uses the shortest wrapped path: when the
   seam-crossing route to the objective is shorter than the raw line, the chosen
   bearing points at the wrapped duplicate; when the raw line is already
   shortest, the chosen bearing is unchanged from today's behaviour.
3. Unit tests cover **each of the four edges** (left/right/top/bottom): the
   wrapped bearing is chosen when it is shorter, and an edge-crossing direction
   is safe when it does not otherwise threaten.
4. Hysteresis at nearly-equal raw/wrapped paths: a test drives a sequence of
   ticks where the two route lengths swap by a tiny margin each tick and asserts
   the committed objective duplicate does not oscillate.
5. The human-like governor's reaction cadence, W/A/D control mapping and human
   thrust presses are unchanged; existing steering/bot integration tests stay
   green apart from the deliberately updated "never wraps" assertion, which is
   re-stated as "still brakes to a controlled stop".
6. The changed-scope test gate passes via `/skill:test` (build → test → commit
   order) with tests written first.

## Key Files

- `src/ai/framework/competent/steering.ts` — `evaluateDirection`, `bearingTo`,
  `chooseSteeringDirection`.
- `src/ai/botDecision.ts` — `evaluateVector` and the legacy target-bearing path.
- `src/ai/framework/competent/steering.test.ts`,
  `src/ai/botDecision.test.ts` — per-edge wrap tests (written first).
- `src/ai/botSteering.integration.test.ts` — updated "never wraps" assertion plus
  seam-crossing scenarios.
- `src/ai/framework/competent/competentBot.integration.test.ts` — wrap scenario.

## Dependencies

Blocked by the wrap-geometry primitives child (shared wrapped delta/bearing +
hysteresis must exist first).

## Out of scope

`wallMargin` removal from tunables, style fitting and the tuning UI (separate
child); aim/intercept, nearest-selection, threat prediction and eval parity
(separate children).

# Seam-aware aim and intercept

Parent: "Bot should be aware of screen wrap around" (AH-0MVMISF0Q00314LG) — AC2
(aim half).

## Goal (user story)

As a **player**, I want the demo bot to aim and fire at an enemy along the
shortest wrapped path — including off one edge to arrive from the opposite edge
— so engagements play out across the whole wrap-around arena.

## Context

Aim maths is raw Euclidean today:

- `bearingTo` (`src/ai/framework/competent/steering.ts`) — `normalise(to - from)`;
- `interceptPoint` (same module) — lead solve on raw deltas;
- the legacy aim/aim-delta path in `src/ai/botDecision.ts` — `atan2` on raw
  deltas.

The enemy side already aims on the torus via `aimVectorToTarget` /
`wrappedAxisDelta` (`src/scenes/core/enemyTargeting.ts`, used by
`Scout.tryFireAimedBullet`), so the bot currently fights a wrap-aware opponent
with a wrap-blind gun — a systematic disadvantage once enemy wrap lands.

## Scope

1. `bearingTo` and `interceptPoint` compute their deltas along the shortest
   wrapped path (per-axis wrapped delta), with the bot's
   `playfieldWidth`/`playfieldHeight`; both accept the wrap model without
   changing their existing signatures' call sites more than necessary (a
   `WrapWorld`/tunables argument).
2. The intercept solve predicts the target on the torus: the predicted point is
   the target's position advanced by its velocity, then the *route* to it is the
   shortest wrapped one, so a lead solution that must cross a seam is still
   produced. Stationary targets reduce exactly to the wrapped bearing.
3. Legacy aim in `src/ai/botDecision.ts` uses the same shared wrapped maths
   (delegating to the shared module, no second implementation).
4. Behaviour is bit-identical when the raw line is already the shortest path.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Seam-aware aim and targeting — aim and target selection run on the torus: `bearingTo`/`interceptPoint` and the legacy aim compute deltas along the shortest wrapped path.
2. Aim runs on the torus: `bearingTo` and `interceptPoint`
   (`src/ai/framework/competent/steering.ts`) and the legacy aim compute in
   `src/ai/botDecision.ts` compute deltas along the shortest wrapped path, using
   the shared wrap-geometry primitives (no copied seam maths).
3. When the wrapped route to a target is shorter than the raw line, the returned
   aim angle equals the wrapped-path angle (test asserts the exact expected
   heading for a target across each of the four edges); firing off one edge
   arrives from the opposite edge.
4. When the raw line is already shortest, the aim angle is unchanged from the
   pre-change behaviour (regression test on a representative non-seam geometry).
5. `interceptPoint` leads a moving target across the seam: a test with a target
   whose velocity carries it over an edge returns the wrapped intercept point and
   converges (iteration count honoured), while a stationary target reduces to the
   wrapped bearing.
6. The legacy decision layer's aim output is byte-for-byte the pre-change value
   for a non-seam geometry (golden assertion in `src/ai/botDecision.test.ts`).
7. The changed-scope test gate passes via `/skill:test` (build → test → commit
   order) with tests written first.

# Build Candidate D — Hangar War (the outer loop)

Follow-on to **We need an outer loop (AH-0MVNSSY9L001P1CC)**, whose deliverable
(`docs/OUTER_LOOP_CANDIDATES.md`) the producer reviewed and closed by choosing
**Candidate D — Hangar War** on 2026-10-29 (`discovered-from:AH-0MVNSSY9L001P1CC`).
This item turns that chosen design into a playable, shippable build. The design
rationale, comparison and the agreed adjustments live in
`docs/OUTER_LOOP_CANDIDATES.md` (Candidate D) and GDD §8; they are the
requirements of record for this item.

## Goal (user story)

As a player, I want my runs to add up to a war I can win — a hangar worth
defending, a ring of hexes around it, and weapons I discover by beating the bosses
that wield them — so that losing a run costs me a ship and its salvage, not my
progress, and so that "beating the boss" is a milestone on the way to holding the
ring rather than the end of everything.

As the producer, I want Candidate D shipped in the order the design recommends —
**Candidate B's MVP (hangar economy) first, then the first hex ring** — so that if
the ring disappoints in play, the hangar stands alone as a complete outer loop and
no work is wasted.

## Scope (from the chosen design)

**Two outer-loop progression axes running together:**
1. **The war on the map** — a hex grid whose first **ring of six hexes** surrounds
   the hangar; which hexes are held, which hold a defending bot, and how aggressive
   the frontier is.
2. **The range of the fleet** — the hangar: hulls, starting weapons, loadouts and
   permanent modifiers bought with banked salvage.

**The capture cycle:** attack a **weak** neighbouring hex → collect salvage →
defeat its **boss** → receive a **new kind of power-up or weapon** into the hangar
→ **leave a bot** flying one of your hulls to defend the hex.

**The frontier:** between runs the AI's border aggression rises and it can
**retake** a held hex unless the player defeats the attacking neighbour. A lost
*run* is still final (ship and unbanked salvage gone); the hangar never is.
Hex defence, mineral accrual and the aggression tick are **algorithmic
resolutions over stored strength numbers** — no live simulated battle.

**Entry surface (producer decision 2026-10-30, Q1 = a):** the hangar war is
reached from its **own top-level menu entry**; **Play Game keeps running the
shipped classic campaign** exactly as today and **Continue — Level N keeps
resuming the arcade run checkpoint**. The two modes share the run code
(`PlayScene` + shared core) but never share session or checkpoint state — a
hex deployment cannot overwrite the arcade checkpoint, and vice versa.

## Agreed design adjustments (2026-10-29 producer review — requirements)

1. **Ring timing is an evening's play, not a grind.** MVP (one ring, six hexes)
   targets **40–60 minutes** for a semi-skilled player: 6 × ≈5-minute
   deployments (≈30 min) plus build/salvage time and a few losses. **Ring 2 is
   larger — 12 hexes**, ≈60 minutes of deployments plus 10–40 minutes of builds
   and losses (~70–100 min). Later rings grow again (ring *n* holds 6*n* hexes),
   so the campaign gets progressively longer, not repetitive.
2. **Boss and weapon strengths are known ahead (MVP).** Before committing to a
   hex the player can see what its boss is, what it is strong/weak against, and
   which hex grants which weapon — enabling deliberate strategy ("take that hex → I
   get the weapon that counters the boss threatening my home hex"). Going beyond
   strategic weapon grants is **out of scope for the MVP**; it is the backlog below.
3. **One hex holds the new weapon — and it is the hardest in the ring.** The other
   five hexes grant upgrades/strength. Players may rush the hard hex and push into
   the next ring (risking losses) or grind the weaker hexes and secure the ring
   first — **different play styles must all be viable** (strategists, grinders,
   completers).
4. **Starting kit clarification.** The *fleet* starts minimal (one basic hull, one
   starting weapon, no hangar modifiers), but the *run* keeps the shipped middle
   loop in full: the six shared loadout slots (any mix of power-up and weapon
   kinds) plus the two slot-free kinds, **Extra Life** and **Mystery UFO**. Do not
   strip the shipped in-run variety to create the outer loop's scarcity.
5. **Post-MVP mitigation backlog (design captured, not MVP):** special missions
   with special rewards (e.g. a new hull type with extra hit points or extra
   upgrade bays), upgraded bots with special skills that are more effective
   against certain enemy/boss types, and further variety so the ring is never a
   six-chore checklist.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. **Hangar slice first (Candidate B's MVP).** Banked salvage (minerals + mini-boss
   cores at the existing checkpoint moments), a persistent hangar with one extra
   hull, three unlockable starting weapons, one permanent modifier, and a
   deployment/loadout selector; losing a run forfeits only that run's unbanked
   salvage.
2. **One hex ring.** A hex-grid map screen with the hangar at the centre and a ring
   of six hexes, each showing held/unheld, aggression, its boss, its granted
   weapon/upgrade and any pending attack; ring growth is data-driven **and ring 2
   (12 hexes) is playable in this build**, generated from hex definitions
   (producer decision 2026-10-30, Q3 = a).
3. **Capture cycle.** Taking a hex = a normal run at that hex's aggression, ending
   in the hex boss; defeating the boss banks salvage, grants the hex's weapon or
   upgrade into the hangar, and lets the player leave a bot flying a chosen hull.
   **Ring secured = every hex of the current ring held** (producer decision
   2026-10-30, Q2 = a); the massed hangar assault and the hangar-falls lose state
   are deferred, see *Out of scope*.
4. **Algorithmic defence + frontier tick.** A pure resolver decides holds/falls from
   stored numbers (defender rating vs attacking force × aggression); one frontier
   tick between runs raises border aggression and can retake a hex; the defence
   report shows the numbers that produced every result.
5. **Boss-granted discovery.** A hex boss demonstrates the weapon it grants; the
   entry appears in the hangar only after the boss is defeated (Rule 2), with the
   six-slot, Extra Life and Mystery UFO behaviour of the shipped run unchanged
   (Rule 1 clarification).
6. **Known-ahead intel, visible.** Hex bosses, their weaknesses and the weapon each
   hex grants are readable before the player commits to a deployment.
7. **Timing targets.** One-ring MVP is completable in 40–60 minutes by a
   semi-skilled player; ring 2 (12 hexes) lands at ≈70–100 minutes; the timing is
   recorded in the GDD and measured with the headless eval arena
   (`src/ai/eval/arena.ts` per-run durations, summed per ring).
8. **Playstyles supported.** A rush through the weapon hex into the next ring, and a
   full grind of the ring before pushing, are both viable and neither is strictly
   dominant; the difficulty curve makes the aggressive line riskier but faster.
9. **Gym coverage and parity.** Hangar economy, defence resolver and frontier clock
   ship as pure logic exercised in a `GymHangar`/`GymHexWar` scene; any new hull,
   weapon or bot behaviour runs the **same code** in gym and game (AGENTS.md
   gym↔game parity, `docs/GYM_PARITY.md` updated).
10. **Attract mode never stalls.** The demo bot traverses or skips the map, hangar
    and defence report (auto-pick weakest hex, auto-buy cheapest useful unlock) and
    there is no live defence battle to stall in.
11. **Persistence.** One versioned `localStorage` key for hangar + ring under GDD
    §6.6 rules (defensive parse, no backend, injectable store), with a migration
    note; a partial ring is never discarded.
12. **Additive entry surface.** The main menu gains a **Hangar War** entry;
    **Play Game still starts the shipped classic 10-level campaign** and
    **Continue — Level N still resumes the arcade run checkpoint**, with no
    shared session state between the modes (producer decision 2026-10-30,

## Goal

Generalise the shipped Phase Shift / Teleport charge engine into **one** charge
pool that serves every consumable, and make a permanent (hold-full) grant add a
charge instead of a level.

Parent: AH-0MVTQMREN009DSFW (Consumable upgrades should not be endless).

## Desired change

- Replace the Phase-Shift/Teleport-specific fields (`_phaseCharges`,
  `_teleportStacks`, `_phaseRechargeTimers`, `_teleportRechargeTimers`) with a
  per-kind pool: `Map<PowerUpId, number>` of available charges plus per-kind
  recharge timers, covering all six consumables.
- Public API (additive; keep the existing Phase Shift / Teleport methods as thin
  delegates so current tests and consumers keep working):
  - `consumeConsumableCharge(id)` — spends exactly one charge; returns `false`
    at zero; starts a recharge timer whose duration is the level-derived
    interval **at the moment of consumption**.
  - `consumableCharges(id)` / `consumableChargeCap(id)` /
    `consumableRechargeTime(id)` / `consumableRechargeRemaining(id)`.
  - `grantConsumableCharge(id, count)` — clamped grant used by the hold-full
    path; grants never exceed the cap and never bank while full.
- `collect(id, true)` for a consumable adds exactly one charge and **does not
  increment the permanent grant count** (so `getPermanentLevel` and
  `getEffectiveLevel` stay unchanged, which is what the hold-full pricing and
  every level consumer read). `_phasePermanent` generalises to a per-kind
  "owned" flag so an empty pool still reports ownership.
- `tickRecharge(dt)` advances every kind's timers, is frame-rate independent
  (a long frame returns as many charges as the elapsed time warrants, remainder
  carried, no banking past the cap) and remains the **only** regeneration
  driver. `reset()` clears every pool and timer.
- Field-pickup grants keep the shipped per-kind semantics for now (producer
  decision 2 / PD5); only the permanent path changes in this child.

## Acceptance Criteria
### Parent-AC traceability (restated from AH-0MVTQMREN009DSFW)

- AC-1 — *Covers parent AC1 (restated):* **AC1 — Permanent grant adds a charge, never a level.** For every consumable
- AC-2 — *Covers parent AC2 (restated):* **AC2 — Charge caps and regeneration follow the agreed configuration.** The


- AC1 — For each of the six consumables, `collect(id, permanent = true)` leaves
  `getPermanentLevel(id)` and `getEffectiveLevel(id)` unchanged and increases
  `consumableCharges(id)` by exactly one. One test per kind.
- AC2 — The grant clamps at the level-derived cap: a grant on a full pool is
  discarded, and no charge is banked while the pool is full (a partially spent
  pool does not accumulate credit for the downtime). Test per kind at cap.
- AC3 — Cap and interval resolve from the catalogue: level 0 gives Shield 1 /
  45 s, Thorn Field 2 / 12 s, Phase Shift 1 / 30 s, Teleport 1 / 15 s,
  Force Field 3 / 45 s, Mystery UFO 1 / 30 s; one levelled point per kind moves
  cap and time in the documented direction.
- AC4 — `consumeConsumableCharge` spends one charge, returns `false` on an empty
  pool, and starts a timer with the level-derived duration at consumption time;
  the spend → empty → regenerate → re-use cycle is covered per kind.
- AC5 — `tickRecharge` is the only regeneration path: no charge returns without
  a tick; many small ticks and one long tick produce the same result; elapsed
  over-cap credits do not bank; `reset()` clears pools and timers.
- AC6 — The existing Phase Shift / Teleport public methods still behave exactly
  as before (their current tests pass unmodified), proving the generalisation is
  behaviour-preserving for the shipped kinds.
- AC7 — Unit tests are written first in this child (red locally, green at
  commit); no test in the repository is left failing.

## Constraints

- **Pure and deterministic.** The store stays free of scene/storage coupling so
  the game and every gym share one model.
- **No clawback.** An expiring temporary window never removes a granted charge.
- **No new pools per scene.** All six kinds live in this one store.

## Key Files

- `src/powerups/powerUpLevels.ts`
- `src/powerups/powerUpLevels.test.ts`

## Dependencies

- Blocked by the catalogue/axes child (consumable set + new axes must exist).

## Goal (user story)

As an implementer, I want a controlled A/B of the same clip length recorded inside and outside the served repository root, so I can tell whether the 661.0 MiB peak came from the in-page fallback probe or from process-lifetime accumulation across a batch — and record the answer **before** any code changes.

Parent: **AH-0MVOJ76MJ0039HNE**. This item is the measurement-first gate that Appendix Q2 = **A** decided; the serving children (2–7 of the plan) are blocked on it.

## Why this gates everything

The cited artefacts (`/tmp/ah-soak/batch-1..5.diagnostics.json`, `capture-output/soak/soak-streamed2.diagnostics.json`) are gone, and the original comparison varied two things at once: the **probe source** (in-page fallback vs streamed) *and* the **batch composition** (5-clip batch outside the root vs a single 600 s clip inside it). The longest single run in that batch peaked at 464.4 MiB, so a fix aimed at the wrong variable would buy nothing.

## Procedure (measurement only — no code changes)

Baseline = the current `dev` capture tool, unmodified.

Arm A/B — isolates the **probe source** (one clip per run, same length):

1. In-root: `npm run capture -- --diagnostics --duration 420000 --output capture-output/ab/inside-root.webm`
2. Out-of-root: `npm run capture -- --diagnostics --duration 420000 --output /tmp/ab/outside-root.webm`

The documented soak table measures a 420 s clip at ≈37.8 MB, i.e. above the 32 MiB stream threshold, so the in-root arm takes the probe route the docs cover and the out-of-root arm takes the in-page fallback.

Arm C/D — isolates **batch accumulation**, only if A/B leaves the cause ambiguous:

3. 5-clip batch out-of-root: `npm run capture -- --count 5 --max-duration 1800000 --diagnostics --output /tmp/ab/batch.webm`
4. 5-clip batch in-root: `npm run capture -- --count 5 --max-duration 1800000 --diagnostics --output capture-output/ab/batch-in.webm`

Record for **every clip**: `probeSource`, `probeSourceReason`, `node.peakRssBytes`, `node.peakRssAtMs`, clip bytes, `page.heapUsedBytes`. For batch arms also record the RSS at each clip **start**, because the filed 661.0 MiB peak was at a clip start — carried over from the previous clip's end-of-clip probe.

## Decision rule (must be applied, not glossed)

- **Fallback is the cause** — the out-of-root peak is materially above the in-root peak and lands at or after the fallback probe: record the numbers and the serving children proceed.
- **Fallback is exonerated** — the arms are comparable, or the peak is plain accumulation across clips: **stop**, implement nothing from the serving children, comment the numbers on the parent, mark the parent `needsProducerReview` (`wl reviewed AH-0MVOJ76MJ0039HNE true`) and recommend the re-scope (documentation correction only). This is the parent's own instruction: "If the AC1 measurement exonerates the fallback, stop and re-scope with the producer before implementing step 2."

## Acceptance criteria

1. A controlled A/B is run on unchanged `dev` with the same clip length inside vs outside the served repository root, and the per-clip `probeSource` plus `node.peakRssBytes` for each arm are recorded as a comment on the parent work item.
2. The measured cause is stated explicitly — fallback probe or process-lifetime accumulation — with the numbers that separate them, and the excluded alternative is named in the same comment.
3. If the fallback is exonerated, the finding is recorded on the parent and the parent is flagged for producer review before any serving change starts; if the fallback is the cause, the finding explicitly unblocks the fix children.
4. No production code, test or documentation file is changed by this item (measurement only), and the `.diagnostics.json` artefacts the numbers came from are named by path in the comment so the figure has provenance.

**Key Files:**

- `scripts/capture-gameplay.mjs` — the capture CLI, `--count`/`--duration`/`--output` and `probeSourceReason`
- `scripts/capture-diagnostics.mjs` — `sampleRss`, the heartbeat samples and the `.diagnostics.json` artefact

# Interruption seam and hermetic crash-path tests

**Parent:** AH-0MVVH57LL00038WQ — Recorder silently loses a session when the browser is closed instead of Ctrl+C.
**Slice:** test-first — this child lands the testable seam plus the interruption/lost-message behaviour that child 2 (checkpointed partial capture) and child 3 (usage/docs) build on.

## Goal

As a **maintainer of the recording tooling**, I want the interruption path to be a testable seam (injected page/fs/clock), so the crash path cannot regress into a raw Playwright stack again.

Today `main()` in `scripts/record-session.mjs` inlines the poll loop and the single post-loop buffer read/write, and only SIGINT/SIGTERM are treated as stops. A `page.waitForTimeout` / `page.evaluate` rejection from a closed page escapes to the top-level handler, prints the raw Playwright message and exits 1 with nothing written and no path named. `scripts/record-session.test.ts` cannot reach any of that without a real browser.

## Scope

- Extract from `main()` and export, fully injectable (page `evaluate`, fs writes, clock):
  - `runRecordingWaitLoop({ evaluate, stop, now, wait, maxDurationMs, pollMs, auto })` → a **stop reason** (`'sigint'`, `'run_end'`, `'max_duration'`, `'target_closed'`), classifying a thrown target-closed failure as `'target_closed'` and consulting `page.isClosed()` / `browser.isConnected()` where available (match the known target-closed message family; any unknown failure defaults to the interruption path, never a raw stack).
  - The interruption finaliser: on `'target_closed'` with nothing captured, print exactly one actionable line naming the resolved output path that was not written plus the Ctrl+C procedure, and return exit code 1. On a clean stop, write the final recording and remove any partial (partial *creation* is child 2; this child makes the removal/salvage decision point exist and be tested).
- New `scripts/record-session.test.ts` (`@vitest-environment node`, temp dirs via `mkdtempSync`, **no real browser**): injected `evaluate`/fs/clock fakes.
- Declare every new export in `scripts/record-session.d.mts`.
- Reuse, do not reimplement: `readDevTelemetryChunk` / `readDevTelemetryBufferInChunks` from `scripts/capture-gameplay.mjs`; mirror the salvage/partial idiom of `scripts/capture-salvage.mjs` and the `<stem>.partial.*` naming of `scripts/capture-chunk-sink.mjs`.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. **The interruption path is covered by hermetic tests.** New tests (`scripts/record-session.test.ts`, node environment, no real browser — page/fs/clock injected) prove: (a) a target-closed error thrown from the poll loop routes to the salvage path and not to a raw error exit; (b) with zero captured bytes the lost message names the output path and the Ctrl+C procedure; (c) a clean stop writes the final file and removes the partial. `scripts/recording-cli.test.ts` keeps passing.
2. The wait/finalise logic of `scripts/record-session.mjs` is exported as injectable functions (page `evaluate`, fs writes and clock injected) so the crash, salvage and clean-stop paths are covered hermetically in `scripts/record-session.test.ts` — no real browser in the suite.
3. A target-closed error thrown from the poll loop routes to the interruption/rescue path and never surfaces a raw Playwright target-closed message as the only diagnostic; the process exits non-zero.
4. With zero captured bytes the recorder prints exactly one actionable line — `Recording lost: the browser was closed before Ctrl+C — run npm run record and press Ctrl+C to save` — naming the resolved output path that was not written; proven in `scripts/record-session.test.ts`.
5. On a clean stop the final recording is written and no partial file remains, proven in `scripts/record-session.test.ts`.
6. `scripts/record-session.d.mts` declares every newly exported helper and the type check passes.
7. No behavioural change to `--auto`, `--seed`, `--bot`, `--bot-config`, `--json`, `--poll`, `--max-duration` or `balance-stats.json` on the clean path; the printed success lines are unchanged.

- `scripts/record-session.mjs` — wait loop, stop reasons, target-closed classification, interruption finaliser, `--help` block.
- `scripts/record-session.test.ts` *(new)* — the hermetic seam tests.
- `scripts/record-session.d.mts` — declarations for the new exports.
- `scripts/capture-gameplay.mjs` — `readDevTelemetryChunk` / `readDevTelemetryBufferInChunks` (reused, not modified).

# Guard the `--out` write probe against pseudo-filesystems (procfs/sysfs) that block `mkdir`

## Summary

Discovered while re-running the AH-0MVBNLM2V008XC8T verification command set for
AH-0MVSE1PG7006XBZ9 (parent epic AH-0MVIKLOOJ0058Z9B).

Slice 2 (AH-0MVSE18XX006ZG5I) added `ensureWritableOutputDir(dir)`, which probes `--out`
with `mkdirSync(dir, {recursive: true})` + a sentinel write before the SSR core boots or any
sweep runs. That removes the *sweep-first* cost, but the parent epic's exact negative probe
still does not fail fast:

```
node scripts/evaluate.mjs --tune --set enemy-configs.csv boss.health=7 \
  --games 2 --ticks 200 --out /proc/nope/x
```

Measured on 2026-10-31 in worktree `wl-AH-0MVSE1PG7006XBZ9-…` (dev @ aef43beef):

| Probe | Result |
|---|---|
| `--out /proc/nope/x` | **blocked for the full 60 s external `timeout`** (exit 124 from `timeout`), no stderr, no journal, CSV untouched |
| `--out /dev/null/x` (ENOTDIR) | exit 2, `output directory not writable: /dev/null/x (ENOTDIR)`, **0.458 s** |
| `--out <chmod 0500>/artifacts` (EACCES) | exit 2, `output directory not writable: … (EACCES)`, **0.380 s** |

Isolated confirmation that the block is the kernel, not the CLI:

```bash
$ timeout -k 2 10 node -e 'const fs=require("fs");
  console.log(JSON.stringify(fs.statfsSync("/proc")));
  fs.mkdirSync("/proc/nope/x", {recursive:true}); console.log("mkdir returned");'
{"type":40864,"bsize":4096,...}          # 40864 == 0x9fa0 == PROC_SUPER_MAGIC
# ...then the process never returns: killed by `timeout` (exit 124)
```

So a `mkdir` (even recursive, i.e. a `stat`-only path when it already exists) on procfs blocks
indefinitely in this environment, and no JS-level timeout can interrupt it — the call never
yields. The only way to make the documented repro fail fast is to **never call `mkdir` on a
pseudo-filesystem**.

## Goal (user story)

As a developer running the tune-loop verification I want the `--out` validation to reject
procfs/sysfs-style targets *before* touching them, so the documented negative probe
(`--out /proc/nope/x`) fails in well under a second with the standard diagnostic instead of
hanging until an external kill.

## Expected behaviour

- `ensureWritableOutputDir(dir)` first resolves the nearest **existing** ancestor of `dir` and
  reads its filesystem type with `fs.statfsSync`. When that type is a known non-writable
  pseudo-filesystem, it returns `{ok: false, reason}` **without calling `mkdirSync`**:
  `output directory not writable: /proc/nope/x (unsupported filesystem type 0x9fa0)`.
- Known pseudo-filesystems to reject (magic numbers, documented in the code):
  procfs `0x9fa0`, sysfs `0x62656572`, debugfs `0x64626720`, tracefs `0x74726163`,
  cgroup `0x27e0eb`, cgroup2 `0x63677270`, devpts `0x1cd1`, securityfs `0x73636673`,
  configfs `0x62656570`, bpf `0xca7baf3d`, nsfs `0x6e736673`.
- Fail-open: when `statfsSync` is unavailable (older Node) or throws, the guard is skipped and
  the existing `mkdir` probe runs unchanged — no regression on normal filesystems.
- Every existing behaviour is preserved: a writable directory (new or existing) still probes
  `{ok: true}`, and EACCES/ENOTDIR still produce the same diagnostics and exit code 2.
- `--help`/`docs/BALANCING.md` mention the pseudo-filesystem guard and that `/proc/nope/x` is
  the documented negative probe.

## Acceptance criteria

1. `node scripts/evaluate.mjs --tune --set enemy-configs.csv boss.health=7 --games 2 --ticks 200 --out /proc/nope/x`
   exits 2 in **< 2 s** with `output directory not writable` and `unsupported filesystem type`, and
   the balance CSV is byte-identical afterwards (digest recorded in a work-item comment).
2. Unit tests cover: procfs rejected without a `mkdir` attempt (asserted with a `mkdirSync` spy or
   an injected `statfs` seam), sysfs-like magic numbers rejected, a normal tmpdir accepted, and
   the fail-open path when `statfsSync` throws/is absent.
3. Existing fail-fast tests (`scripts/evaluate-failfast.test.ts`) stay green — EACCES, ENOTDIR and
   the happy path are unchanged.
4. `--help` and `docs/BALANCING.md` document the guard; the docs guard
   (`src/ai/eval/balancingDocs.test.ts`) asserts it.
5. All tests run under the project test policy (test skill).

## Context

- Parent epic: AH-0MVIKLOOJ0058Z9B (its AC1/AC4 require the `/proc/nope/x` probe to fail fast).
- Depends on slice 2 (AH-0MVSE18XX006ZG5I) which introduced `ensureWritableOutputDir`.
- Blocks slice 5 (AH-0MVSE1PG7006XBZ9) evidence re-run: the "before/after" negative-probe table
  needs the post-fix row to be sub-second rather than "blocked until externally killed".
- Evidence comment on AH-0MVSE1PG7006XBZ9 records the measurements above.
